newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FOREIGN BANKS TO RETURN TO MANILA FOREX MARKET.
newsitem.headline: FOREIGN BANKS TO RETURN TO MANILA FOREX MARKET.

text.p: The board of the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP) agreed to allow six foreign banks to participate again at the Philippine Dealing System (PDS) from Monday, BAP president Deogracias Vistan told Reuters on Friday.
"We agreed to try it out. Observe the market indefinitely," he said.
"We think this is one more step towards normalisation. Obviously, if the market signs continue to normalise, it's no longer trying it out. It's there as a permanent commitment," he said.

The six foreign banks - Citibank, Deutsche Bank, Bank of America, Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp, ING Bank and Standard Chartered Bank - had been requested by the BAP not to participate in the PDS since the peso had a de facto devaluation on July 11.
The PDS is the computerised peso/dollar trading among banks.

The six foreign banks -- units of Citicorp, Deutsche Bank AG, BankAmerica Corp, HSBC Holdings ING Groep NV and Standard Chartered Plc -- had been requested by the BAP not to participate in the PDS since the peso had a de facto devaluation on July 11.
The BAP had also requested foreign banks with large requirements, such as $10 million or higher, to source these first with the forward contract window of the Philippine central bank, Vistan said.
Foreign banks were also asked not to close their open positions on non-deliverable forwards through the spot market and instead use the central bank's forward facility, he said.

"We are looking here at a market that has just recovered, or is just recovering. We just want to make sure there is no pent-up demand that is immediately brought upon the market," he said, adding that banks may not easily meet those large requirements because they have to maintain long dollar positions only up to five percent of capital.

"Our position is that foreign banks have dollars to sell and dollars to buy. We assume on balance the effects will be the same. They (foreign banks) are saying some days it's sell and some days it's buy," he said when asked if foreign banks would be net sellers or buyers of dollars in the market.
Vistan said the central bank had been advised of the BAP's decision.
"The central bank will not commit (to) make forward contracts available. But they do appreciate being asked before the foreign banks go to the PDS," he said.
The peso, along with other currencies in the region, was severely hit by speculation and the central bank spent nearly $2 billion in a futile defence since April.
The pressure remained even after the de facto devaluation but bankers said it seemed to have eased this week.
